content.title: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) — extracted page content
content.summary: Discussion of long-term functional impairment after pulmonary embolism (PE) and a detailed section (10.2) on epidemiology, pathophysiology, and natural history of CTEPH, including reported incidence estimates and a multicentre Swiss screening study.

sections.heading: Functional impairment after PE
sections.text: Older and more recent cohort studies suggest muscle deconditioning, excess body weight and cardiopulmonary comorbidity largely explain frequently reported dyspnoea and exercise limitation after acute PE. Independent predictors of reduced functional exercise capacity and quality of life over time included female sex, higher body mass index, history of lung disease, higher pulmonary artery systolic pressures on the 10-day echocardiogram, and larger main pulmonary artery diameter on baseline CTPA. Pulmonary function tests and echocardiographic results at follow-up were largely within normal limits in patients with and without reduced maximal aerobic capacity. A lack of association between exercise impairment and persistent RV dilation or dysfunction was reported in a small study of survivors of massive/submassive PE. Ongoing prospective studies in large numbers of patients are needed to identify predictors of functional and/or haemodynamic impairment after acute PE.

sections.heading: 10.2 Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
sections.text: CTEPH is caused by persistent obstruction of pulmonary arteries by organized thrombi, leading to flow redistribution and secondary remodelling of the pulmonary microvascular bed. The hallmark is fibrotic transformation of a pulmonary arterial thrombus causing fixed mechanical obstruction and overflow of open pulmonary arterial beds.

sections.heading: 10.2.1 Epidemiology, pathophysiology, and natural history
sections.text: Reported cumulative incidence of CTEPH after a symptomatic PE event ranges widely, between 0.1% and 9.1% within the first 2 years; the wide range reflects referral bias, paucity of early symptoms, and difficulty differentiating acute PE from pre-existing CTEPH. A prospective multicentre observational screening survey in Switzerland (patients with acute PE from 11 centres, March 2009–November 2016) screened for CTEPH at 6, 12 and 24 months using a stepwise algorithm including a phone-based dyspnoea survey, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), right heart catheterization, and radiological confirmation. Of 508 patients assessed for CTEPH screening over 2 years, CTEPH incidence following PE was 3.7 per 1000 patient-years, with a 2-year cumulative incidence of 0.79%. In Germany, the incidence of CTEPH in 2016 was estimated at 5.7 per million adult population.
